```Welcome to this video on security information and event management. As part of security operations, we certainly talked about the need for logging and monitoring, and a SIEM system, a security information and event manager, will help with this greatly. Now, the SIEM system is used for real-time analysis of security related events and SIEM systems are often used for advanced level threat detection using log data that's been collected from multiple system components. So again, if you recall from the logging and monitoring video, we talked about decentralized and centralized collection and this is what we're talking about, we're bringing everything into a central point and then the SIEM system can perform a variety of functions to analyze that log data and generate it into a format that would be helpful for advanced level detection. And you'll often find SIEM systems in security operation centers or SOCs and other large enterprise networks. It's not to say you won't find 'em in smaller systems, 'cause I have certainly deployed them on smaller systems throughout my career. The thing with SIEMs is because of the sheer amount of data that is being collected by these different components, you need some kind of tool to gather it all, analyze it all, and sort through all the different noise that's out there. And this is going to help you find those potential threats and attacks that are happening throughout the system and that's what the SIEM is designed to do, 'cause oftentimes they implement machine learning or artificial intelligence techniques that will help you narrow down all of the information and present it in the format you need to see it on a user interface and that will help you make realtime decisions about threats and possible attacks in the system. Now, SIEM systems have been around for a while in some form or another. It started off as a security information manager or SIM, this was used to gather logs into a central location or repository, also called a log server. And then there was also a security event manager, or SEM, that SIEM was used to correlate and analyze those logs for potential security events. Now, back in the day I'll say, this was a single product and this was a single product and they worked together, now the SIEM is traditionally merged together and now it's one product. And again, you might hear it called SIEM in the industry, but in reality it the actual acronym for it is SEIM, S-E-I-M and the reason it's called SIEM is because S-I-M is SIM and S-E-M is SEM, makes sense, let's stay with that right now. One thing I want you to know about SIEMs is that this is an industry product, there's no standard here for how you implement them, there's no standard for how you configure them. Really what's going to happen is you're going to have industry standards or regulations that are going to have controls that specify real-time monitoring, real-time alert status or something like that, and some controls might literally say, "You need a SIEM system," but they are not going to determine or dictate how to configure them. So really what we're looking at doing is the focus becomes how the logs are collected and the amount of logs that are collected. Then we're going to focus on displaying those things on a user interface, now, that's the part that's not going to be standardized. This has to do with preference, what are you looking at in your system or what are your senior managers most concerned with? Or what is your industry most concerned with? And that's where our focus lies. So every SIEM system might be operating just a little bit different than the other because there's no traditional way to do this. But there are traditional deployments that you need to be familiar with, how these SIEM systems are configured. The first way we can do it is agentless, where we receive log data from hosts without a need for any other software or we can install an agent where we have to install some specialized software that's going to transmit the log data back to the log server. Now I'll say about 10 years ago, this was the way it's done, nowadays, there's a lot of ways to do agentless SIEMs. Now I've used a variety of them, most of them are agent-based and the deployment method is really going to be based on the vendor. So if you choose to go with Elastic Stack, they're going to do an agent-based deployment. There's also a way to do an agentless based deployment, but in my experience, the agent-based has been the most successful. Now again, we had the SIM and the SEM, the S-I-M and the S-E-M. The SIM was the collector and aggregator, this collects the messages and logs from the various host, then we had the SEM, which was the correlation engine that creates the audit trail from the various messages and logs, these are now combined into one system. So the SIEM systems will have both capabilities on board, they have the collection aggregation and they also have the correlation. In addition, they have the alerting and reporting where you get alerts, you can get email alerts, you can get console alerts, you can get a lot of different alert messages or you can create reports based on configured settings. Whatever you've set it, you can generate reports. Oftentimes when you're working in an op center, whether it's a security op center, a SOC, or a network op center, a NOC, you have to generate ports every single day. This gives senior management kind of a situational awareness of what's going on so you'll have to generate the reports. The SIEM systems are excellent for this, they can generate a great report that you can just hand over every single day, you don't have to do a whole lot of work, and it has a lot of data that's relevant to what the senior managers want to see. The SIEM system is also capable of retention and archive, storing those collective messages for whatever the industry standard or governance and regulations have determined. So as they're in archive, of course we want to protect them, but we want to retain them according to our industry standard. And often with the retention and archive, we have data stockpiling, which is we've collected so many logs and all of this different stuff that we're putting it all on the server to allow the SIEM to comb through all of it, to search through all of it and that's where our machine learning and artificial intelligence can really come in handy. When you have a stockpile of data, it can actually sort through all of that and look through all of it and then present the most relevant data according to what it is you want to see. So just an example, this is a dashboard from a SIEM, this is Elastic Stack here and what you're looking at is you're looking at a variety of different charts, graphs, and other things, like down here you have visitors down on the lower right and as you can see, the darker the colors, the more visitors you're having. So there's certain parts in Africa here that we're not getting any visitors, but we have a lot coming from Asia, we have a lot coming from the United States, we have a lot coming from South America. So you can see that, wow, we're getting a lot of hits from these areas, that's going to help, in terms of threat awareness, threat intelligence. Hey, there's a lot of attacks coming out of the United States. Well, if we're getting a lot of visits, this could tell you, right here, this could tell you that we might be at risk and then we have logs and we have visitors, and now we're tracking the OS. If there's a lot of vulnerabilities in a certain OS, we want to know it. In this case, they're a little bit older, XP, there's Windows eight, there's iOS, which is mobile, then there's OSX, which is Mac, apple and then you have Windows seven. Nobody from Windows 10 or anything else is logging in, which, okay, fine, no worries. So you can really set this up to filter on whatever you want it to and you can decorate, I'll call it, "Decorate," you can decorate this dashboard however you want with whatever data is valuable to you and your organization. If you don't care about your visitors, if you don't care about the operating systems, then filter that stuff out, but if you care about logons or logon attempts, then you want to filter that in and display it on your dashboard. That way an analyst that's working in your op center can look at it, see it in real time and see the alerts as well and then they can act upon that information. And again, all of that information is being fed from all these devices, your firewalls are sending all this information, your switches, your storage servers, your infrastructure, your web servers, your applications, everything is being sent to these log servers and within this dashboard, you can filter everything that you want to see based on your industry standards or requirements or any kind of interesting traffic that pertains to what your senior management is most concerned with. Here is a structural summary of the provided video transcript on **Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)** :

### 1. Definition & Core Purpose
- **SIEM** stands for **Security Information and Event Management** (though the acronym is sometimes colloquially ordered as *SEIM*).
- **Primary Use**: Real-time analysis of security-related events for advanced threat detection.
- **Key Function**: Collects log data from multiple system components into a central point, then analyzes and formats it for detection.

### 2. Historical Evolution
- **SIM** (Security Information Manager): Gathered logs into a central repository/log server.
- **SEM** (Security Event Manager): Correlated and analyzed logs for security events.
- **Current State**: SIM and SEM are now merged into a single SIEM product.

### 3. Deployment Context
- Commonly found in **Security Operations Centers (SOCs)** and large enterprise networks, but can also be deployed in smaller systems.
- Uses **machine learning (ML)** and **artificial intelligence (AI)** to filter noise and present relevant data for real-time decisions.

### 4. Lack of Standardization
- SIEM is an **industry product** with **no standard** implementation or configuration.
- Configuration depends on:
  - Industry regulations (e.g., controls requiring real-time monitoring/alerting).
  - Organizational preferences and senior management concerns.
- Result: Every SIEM deployment may operate slightly differently.

### 5. Deployment Methods
- **Agentless**: Receives log data from hosts without additional software.
- **Agent-based**: Requires specialized software on each host to transmit logs.
  - *Note*: Agent-based is noted as more successful in the speaker’s experience; choice often depends on the vendor (e.g., Elastic Stack uses agent-based).

### 6. Core Capabilities of a SIEM System
- **Collection & Aggregation** (inherited from SIM).
- **Correlation Engine** (inherited from SEM) – creates audit trails.
- **Alerting & Reporting** – email/console alerts; generates daily reports for management.
- **Retention & Archive** – stores logs per industry standards/regulations.
- **Data Stockpiling** – large volumes of logs enable ML/AI to search and surface relevant data.

### 7. Example & Dashboard Customization
- **Example Tool**: Elastic Stack dashboard.
- **Dashboard Visualization Examples**:
  - Geographic visitor heatmaps (e.g., traffic from Asia, US, South America).
  - Operating systems of visitors (e.g., Windows XP, Windows 7, iOS, OSX).
- **Customization**: Users can filter what data appears (e.g., logon attempts, specific OS vulnerabilities) based on organizational needs, allowing analysts to view real-time alerts and act.

### 8. Bottom Line for Exam/Certification Preparation
- **Know the purpose** of SIEM.
- **Understand how SIEM works** (collection, correlation, alerting, retention, and dashboard customization).

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on threat intelligence:

## 1. Core Definition & Purpose
- **Threat Intelligence:** Analyzed information used to make threat-based decisions (conclusions drawn from raw data).
- **Threat:** Potential for unwanted harm to personnel or assets.
- **Vulnerability:** Flaw or weakness a threat acts against.
- **Attack Surface:** All possible entry points (people, technology, physical access, etc.) for compromise.

## 2. Key Concepts & Relationships
- **Threat Information** → **Threat Intelligence** = situational awareness.
- Uses risk indicators, performance indicators, etc., to understand security posture.

- Format: Often raw XML.
- **Tools to ingest/interpret:** Yeti, AlienVault.

## 4. Threat Hunting (Proactive Search)
- Definition: Searching for *previously undetected* threats or attacks (goes beyond known alerts).
- Process:
  1. Detect a known threat (e.g., from a threat feed).
  2. Go on the offensive — proactively search systems for impact.
  3. Identify presence → take remedial action.
- **Value:** Enables proactive defense, not just reactive alerts.

## 5. Practical Tools (Examples)
- **Yeti:** Ingests threat feeds; shows malware, domains, crime data; supports threat hunting.
- **AlienVault:** Similar ingestion and hunting capabilities.

## 6. Bottom Line (Key Takeaways)
- Understand **why** we gather threat intelligence.
- Know **threat feeds** and **threat hunting** as they relate to threat intelligence.

These were all techniques or tactics or procedures or whatever that were used in real-world attacks. So this is used to develop threat models and methodologies for any organization. Any organization who wants to use this framework can benefit from it. And it's broken down into specific attack categories with the specific TTPs within each of those categories. Now, one thing to note about this framework is that it is fluid. It is changing frequently. It is always being updated by MITRE. They do a pretty good job keeping it updated because as real-world attacks come in, things are changing. Attackers get smarter. They get craftier. They learn how to do different things. So that's exactly why you don't need to memorize all this or know all of it. What you do need to understand are the different categories and how they're going to be beneficial when it comes to threat modeling. So the first category is Reconnaissance. This is what we do to gather information. This is passive scanning. This is open-source intelligence or OSINT, phishing. A lot of different things happen in the Reconnaissance category. Then you also have Resource Development. This is where they're focused on discovering the different attack vectors. We're looking at different assets. We're trying to figure out how we can possibly get into the system from an attacker's point of view. Then we had the Initial Access, where an attacker initially gains access to the system. How did they get into the system, what account was compromised, those kinds of things. Then we have the Execution, where they're attempting to install or run malware. Some kind of script, some kind of code, whatever it is. The next category is Persistence, where they're maintaining access. You're manipulating accounts, account information, system functions and processes, whatever you need to in order to maintain access. And sometimes, you'll see this referred to as Command and Control as well. Then there's Privilege Escalation, how can you get higher privileges on the system. If you compromise a general user account of just a, you know, a random account, how can you escalate those privileges and get administrator or root level privileges? Then we have Defense Evasion, where we're trying to avoid being detected. We're trying to evade those intrusion detection systems, the endpoint security, different things like that. Then we have Credential Access as the next category, where you're looking to steal account information or steal credentials. In this case, you're trying to find new accounts, trying to find new passwords. That way, you can maintain access. And then we have Discovery, which is to search for more assets to exploit. And part of that is going to be lateral movement, because once you find more assets, we can laterally move throughout the system. And this is east and west in terms of communication versus north and south. North being ingress, south being egress, and east and west being lateral movement. Then we have Collection, where they're gathering all of the target data. In this terms, you're thinking more along the lines of gathering all the data that you're trying to access as part of this attack. And then lastly, we do have Command and Control, where you're taking control of other compromised machines. Again, sometimes maintaining access and command and control get interchanged, but in reality, what you're trying to do is command and take over the system so that you can start compromising more machines. The last two categories we have are Exfiltration, where you're stealing the data, the target data, whatever that might be, and then we have Impact, where you're trying to pretty much impact confidentiality, integrity, or availability. So you're trying to compromise, interrupt, or deny system operations, okay? Now, I know that's a lot of information in terms of the framework. Do you need to know this for the exam? You don't need to know every one of these categories or every one of these things. I'm trying to walk through these just to help you kind of understand where from a threat model perspective you would bring this into play. Now, if you recall all the way back to Domain 1, I showed you Threat Dragon in the Threat Modeling video. Now, Threat Dragon is just a tool that you can use to create a threat model. So looking at this threat model we have here, we have a web application, we have a browser, and then we have some backend processes that are happening over here. And then you also have the configuration, you have a database, and you have, you know, whatever the worker config is. So in this regard, from a reconnaissance, let's take the first category of the ATT@CK framework, where can someone gather initial information? On websites. So what kind of data is out on the internet? About your organization, about your executives, about you as an administrator maybe. So that's the first place that we're going to start, is passive reconnaissance. We're going to start doing open-source intelligence gathering. We're going to start looking for information that's relevant to the company. All right, now, from a threat modeling perspective, you can't really do much about it because a lot of those databases are maintained by external parties. But you can contact them and ask them to pull that data off of their website because it's your data. You have the right to do that. Now, in terms of resource development being the next category, now what are we talking about? We're talking about attack vectors, so what would be the attack vector. Well, in terms of this web application, it'd be a browser trying to get to that web app. And then you have these modeled out right here, a web request, and then there's going to be a web response that comes back. So maybe we validate or we authenticate that web request before we provide a response. That's how we start to build our threat models. This is how you start to understand where everything is happening from a big picture, not just "We need to lock this down," or "We need to scan this." Now you're taking a look at the overall performance of the system and all of the different vectors that are going to come into the system. The same being said about what about an attack vector if somebody compromised the web app and now they want to get to the database. What's the attack vector? Well, it's going to be an SQL query, right here. So now maybe we want to authenticate that SQL query before we allow it just to go through. Things like that come into play. And then initial access, where are they going to get access. Well, access is definitely going to be at the web application level. We can't control the web browser 'cause that's outside of our control. The database, they could get access to that. They could also maybe even get access to the configuration, but that's not really what an attacker's looking to gain access for. So maybe that's a lower risk in that regard. Then the execution, where would they install malware, scripts, root kits, whatever they're trying to install? Well, it would be on the server right here that's hosting this web application and on the server that's hosting the database, all those different things. And then once it's been installed, they need to execute it. How is it going to reach out? Now we want to talk about maybe white listing all of our protocols. So we want to allow only specific protocols to go to and from this database or this backend process. Maybe this messaging protocol that's being run up here needs to be filtered to make sure that we're restricting how that malware or how that code could spread. Then we also have persistence, how would they maintain access. Well, how many accounts are on that database server? How many accounts are on that web server? And then we also have escalation, are there privileged accounts on there, and what are they set up like? What's their password management practices like? What about defenses? So we have a defense invasion, that's the next category. What about endpoint security firewalls? What's going on on all these different devices? And then we have the credential access. Again, we're going back to the accounts, account management, access control, password management. All of these things start working in. And with the ATT@CK Framework, which makes it very, very effective, is it's an easy reference point to get you to start thinking about those TTPs that are being currently used. And, I mean, trust me, when you start doing threat modeling, you don't really think of all these things. It takes a little while to work through 'em all. So when you reference this framework, it can help jar your memory, it can help inspire you to look in different areas where you're looking at discovery, like what's going to be on those systems? Can you find other systems like if you're on the database server? Can you do some kind of query, or can you do a trace route or a ping or something like that that will identify some other servers? Is there a place to laterally move? Are there multiple database servers? Is the web server and the database on the same network so someone can laterally move between them? And then of course, when we talk about collection, which is that next category, how valuable is that data? Is that data properly protected? Is it encrypted at rest? Is it open? Is it sitting there static? Is it, you know, in an open directory that's world-readable? All these things start to come into play, okay? For the CISSP exam, what you need to understand is that this framework is out there, okay? So the bottom line is you really want to understand the purpose of the MITRE ATT&CK Framework and how it can help you in the threat modeling aspect.```

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on the **MITRE ATT&CK Framework** for the CISSP exam.

### 1. Overview & Purpose
- **Context:** Part of CISSP Domain 1 (Threat Intelligence).
- **What it is:** An open knowledge base of real-world attacker **TTPs** (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures).
- **Key characteristics:** Large, fluid, frequently updated by MITRE based on new attacks.
- **Exam expectation:** Understand its *purpose* and how it helps **threat modeling**, not memorize all details.

### 2. The 14 ATT&CK Categories (Tactics)
The framework organizes attacker behavior into these sequential categories:

| Phase | Tactic | Description |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| 1 | **Reconnaissance** | Passive scanning, OSINT, phishing to gather info. |
| 2 | **Resource Development** | Discovering attack vectors and assets to exploit. |
| 3 | **Initial Access** | First entry into the system (compromised account, etc.). |
| 4 | **Execution** | Running malware, scripts, or code. |
| 5 | **Persistence** | Maintaining access (manipulating accounts/processes). |
| 6 | **Privilege Escalation** | Gaining higher privileges (e.g., admin/root). |
| 7 | **Defense Evasion** | Avoiding detection (IDS, endpoint security). |
| 8 | **Credential Access** | Stealing account info/passwords. |
| 9 | **Discovery** | Searching for more assets to exploit (leads to lateral movement). |
| 10 | **Collection** | Gathering target data. |
| 11 | **Command & Control** | Controlling compromised machines to expand attack. |
| 12 | **Exfiltration** | Stealing the target data. |
| 13 | **Impact** | Disrupting confidentiality, integrity, or availability. |

> **Note:** The video notes that Persistence and Command & Control are sometimes used interchangeably but serve distinct roles.

### 3. How to Apply the Framework to Threat Modeling
Using a web application threat model (e.g., with Threat Dragon tool):

| ATT&CK Tactic | Practical Threat Modeling Question |
|---------------|--------------------------------------|
| Reconnaissance | What info about the org/execs is publicly available on websites? |
| Resource Development | What are the attack vectors? (e.g., browser → web app, SQL query → database) |
| Initial Access | Where will access be gained? (e.g., web app layer) |
| Execution | Where could malware be installed/executed? (e.g., web server, database server) |
| Persistence | How many accounts exist on those servers? |
| Privilege Escalation | Are there privileged accounts? How are passwords managed? |
| Defense Evasion | What endpoint security/firewalls are in place? |
| Credential Access | Account management, access control, password policies. |
| Discovery / Lateral Movement | Can the attacker move from web server to database server? Same network? |
| Collection | Is data encrypted at rest? World-readable? |
| Exfiltration / Impact | How is data protected during theft or disruption? |

### 4. Key Takeaway for CISSP Exam
- **You do not need to memorize all 14 categories.**
- You **must understand**:
  - The **purpose** of the MITRE ATT&CK Framework.
  - That it provides a reference of real-world TTPs.
  - How it helps **trigger memory and inspire threat modeling** by systematically considering attack vectors and defenses.

```Welcome to this video on the Cyber Kill Chain. On the CISSP exam, you're certainly going to see questions about threat intelligence, feeds, hunting, and even threat modeling. Along those same lines is the Cyber Kill Chain. The Cyber Kill Chain is designed to proactively detect persistent threats. Sometimes this is also called advanced persistent threats. Now the Kill Chain was developed by Lockheed Martin, and this is part of their IDD, the Intelligence Driven Defense model. This is used for the identification and prevention of cyber intrusion activity. The goal of the Cyber Kill Chain is to understand the attacker's action so that you can defend against the attack. So the overall purpose here is stopping adversaries at any stage of the chain. The framework is designed to help you understand the series of events that have to happen as part of an attack, and the idea is to find the link in the chain that we can break in order to defend against that potential attack, okay. So the idea behind this is to understand the aggressor or the attacker's actions, and then if we can break that chain of events, we can defeat or minimize the potential impact of that attack. Now again, this is focused on advanced persistent threat. Advanced being sophisticated, it's a sophisticated level of skill and expertise. These are not script keys, people who are just running tools to see what they can do, these are experienced adversaries, who really, truly know what they're doing. Then you have persistent, which is continue to attack a target over and over, over a period of time. And then we have the threat, the potential for unwanted harm to personnel or an organizational asset. So the goal behind advanced persistent threat or APT is that these attackers or a group of attackers use a variety of different attack vectors, whether it be from the cyber side of things, the physical side of things, and also social engineering as well, they are doing all of this in order to achieve an outcome, whatever their goal is, and they will not stop until they reach their objective. So within the chain, if we can find out where they are in the process, we can stop them before they move to the next step, and that will hopefully minimize the damage or thwart the attack altogether. So first, an attacker has to perform reconnaissance. They have to gather information. They have to try to get names. They have to try to get emails. They have to try to get information about the company, whether it's open source intelligence, OSINT, or whatever it is, they are going to start gathering information. This is going to be done passively, so they're not detected. At this point, they might have enough information to start creating some kind of exploit. This is the weaponization phase, where they're going to start looking at opportunities to start attacking the system. Once they create the exploit and they're confident that this is going to work, they have to deliver or deploy this exploit. So this is the delivery phase of the chain, where they're going to try to send it via phishing email, maybe they're going to try to install it on a website, or maybe they put a thumb drive, a USB drive in a parking lot and hope somebody's going to install it, whatever that might be, but they have to get it deployed. Otherwise, the exploit's not going to work. Once the exploit has been deployed, now they can start taking advantage of the exploitation. So now we can activate the exploit and start taking advantage of the vulnerability and the victims. The next link in the chain is to install some kind of malicious software or malware. Now, we're going to install back doors. We're going to install, just different things, whatever it is we're trying to accomplish, whether it's viruses, it's worms, whatever it is, they're going to try to install this. This might help them with exploitation of data. This might help them with a variety of things. Then we want to maintain access, that is the next step, the command and control. Now, you own the system, you own the asset, and you want to maintain access. That way, you can achieve your outcome, the actions on the objective. Now you have access, you can accomplish whatever your goal is, and now the exploitation has fully taken place, and now this attacker truly owns the system. So at this point, part of this is to use our threat intelligence, our threat hunting, and use everything at our disposal to discover where the attackers are in this chain. And if we detect that maybe they're at the delivery, maybe we're getting a bunch of phishing emails, now we want to look ahead in the chain and see if we can stop an installation, or if we can prevent them from exploiting. We want to stay a step ahead, take that next step, and look forward. That's why it's a proactive framework, because sometimes you will detect it after the malware's already been deployed. Now your job is to focus on breaking link number six, to get them off the system, to keep them from achieving their outcome. And sometimes, you might catch them in the middle of weaponization, maybe they do some active reconnaissance, they start doing some scanning, some footprinting, and you catch 'em at that point. So now what you want to do is stop their deployment, prevent them from deploying. How can you do that? Okay, so part of this is to think proactively. Think ahead in how you could solve this as part of your incident response and incorporate this as part of your threat intelligence gathering. So the bottom line here is to understand advanced persistent threat and also understand the purpose of the Cyber Kill Chain.```

Here’s a structural summary of the provided text on the **Cyber Kill Chain**:

## 1. Context & Relevance
- **Exam relevance**: Appears on CISSP exam (topics: threat intelligence, threat hunting, threat modeling).
- **Purpose**: Proactively detect persistent threats (often called *advanced persistent threats*, APTs).

## 2. Origin & Goal
- **Developed by**: Lockheed Martin.
- **Part of**: Intelligence Driven Defense (IDD) model.
- **Goal**: Identify/prevent cyber intrusions; stop adversaries at any stage of the chain.
- **Core idea**: Understand attacker actions → break one link in the chain → defend against/minimize attack impact.

## 3. Definition of APT
| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Advanced** | Sophisticated skill/expertise (not script kiddies). |
| **Persistent** | Continues attacking target over time. |
| **Threat** | Potential for unwanted harm to personnel/assets. |

APTs use multiple vectors (cyber, physical, social engineering) and persist until objective is achieved.

## 4. The 7 Stages of the Cyber Kill Chain

1. **Reconnaissance** – Passive info gathering (names, emails, OSINT).
2. **Weaponization** – Creating exploit based on gathered intel.
3. **Delivery** – Deploying exploit (phishing, malicious website, USB drop).
4. **Exploitation** – Activating exploit to take advantage of vulnerability.
5. **Installation** – Installing malware (backdoors, viruses, worms).
6. **Command & Control (C2)** – Maintaining access to owned system.
7. **Actions on Objective** – Achieving attacker’s final goal.

## 5. Proactive Defense Strategy
- Use threat intelligence and threat hunting to detect attacker’s **current stage**.
- **Think ahead**: If detection happens at delivery → focus on stopping installation or exploitation.
- If malware already deployed → break link #6 (C2) to prevent objective achievement.
- If caught during weaponization → block deployment.
- Integrate kill chain thinking into **incident response** and **threat intelligence gathering**.

## 6. Bottom Line
- Understand APT behavior.
- Understand the Cyber Kill Chain as a **proactive framework** for breaking attack sequences.

```Welcome to this video on security orchestration, automation, and response. On the CISSP exam, you may see a question about SOAR, Security Orchestration, Automation and Response. And it's exactly how it sounds. It is an automated incident response using a collection of different technologies. So we are combining a lot of different technologies to provide an automated incident response, and that's what SOAR is comprised of. SOAR is designed to reduce the workload of manual incident response by automating this response to common incidents that we might see. This is going to help reduce human error, reduce the overall workload for our analysts, our engineers, and provide for quicker response times. Because SOAR will provide an automatic response that's configured based on threat intelligence, assessment results and more. So the way it works is you're going to collect all of your security data across the entire enterprise or across the system, if you will. You're going to collect this data in regards to users, devices, applications, the infrastructure, and you're going to do this for both on-prem and off-prem solutions. And that could be in the cloud or at a recovery site or whatever it might be. And we would normally use a security information and event manager to do this. This is what we would use to collect the data. Then we would move into the detection where we would try to minimize false positives using good threat intelligence. So as part of the detection, we're focused on all of the data that was collected, and now we want to sort through it and we want to make sure that we're not responding to false positives because that takes a lot of overhead, it takes a lot of analysis and so on. So we want to minimize those as much as possible. So we're going to use analytics to correlate alerts and incidents and minimize the number of events that require a response from us. Then we would use artificial intelligence or machine learning to determine the best course of action based on what information we have in front of us. And lastly, we would respond. We would execute playbook steps to automatically respond and prevent an incident. So this helps us understand the scope and to find the root cause of a potential security threat. Using SOAR we are proactively hunting for security threats across our organization's data sources, and then we're going to minimize all those false positives and then respond to the events that we have remaining. And how we would automate the response here is we would use the playbook. The playbook is a set of actions that automate the investigation and response process. There's also a runbook, which is used to execute the playbook within the source software. So in other words, if an event is detected, the runbook will execute the steps inside the playbook. So some vendors will refer to this differently. There's really no good way to define this, but in actuality, think of the runbook as the script that's going to call everything within the playbook. So if you're familiar with chef as an automation software, you have the cookbook. The cookbook will call recipes, and those recipes will define the configuration. This is very much similar in that regard. Where the runbook is executing the different playbooks, there might be more than one playbook. So in chef speak, this is your cookbook, and playbooks are your recipes. So these are all the different actions to respond to different events. So a runbook might call one, two, or three different playbooks altogether, and now we're going to execute those different steps. And imagine doing this in a manual sense. That is exactly why we use SOAR to orchestrate and automate this response process and remove us from that manual process. Okay, so hopefully this makes sense. Here's an example from D3 Security. They're one of the best in the business when it comes to SOAR. So as you can see, they have their playbook here. This is their email phishing playbook. And within the playbook itself, there's a lot of different steps that take place and a lot of different things that have to happen for the software to orchestrate the process. And that's exactly what the playbook does for us. In the sense of a runbook, the runbook would call this playbook, and it might also call another playbook as a part of this process as well. So when the trigger happens within the system, then it will call the playbooks and then it will execute all the steps you see here. And as you can see, is something high or low, or moderate, or what have you. If it's true and it's high, then it triggers another event and it just goes down the path. So this is how we build our playbooks to orchestrate the security response. Now, you don't need to know all of this for the exam, you just need to know what a runbook and a playbook is used for. I just wanted to give you a demonstration real quick of how these are used within security orchestration and automation response. So the bottom line for this video is to understand the purpose of SOAR and also understand the purpose of the playbook, workbook, or runbook, however you see that terminology depending on the vendor.```

Here’s a **structural summary** of the provided text on **SOAR** (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response):

---

### 1. **Definition & Purpose of SOAR**
- **SOAR** = Security Orchestration, Automation, Response  
- Automated incident response using a collection of technologies  
- Goal: Reduce **manual incident response workload**, human error, analyst/engineer burden, and improve response times  
- Uses threat intelligence, assessment results, etc., to trigger automatic responses  

---

### 2. **How SOAR Works (Step-by-Step)**
1. **Collect**  
   - Gather security data across the entire enterprise (users, devices, apps, infrastructure, on-prem, cloud, recovery sites)  
   - Typically uses a **SIEM** (Security Information and Event Manager)

2. **Detect**  
   - Minimize **false positives** using threat intelligence & analytics  
   - Correlate alerts/incidents to reduce events needing human response

3. **Analyze**  
   - Use **AI / machine learning** to determine best course of action

4. **Respond**  
   - Execute **playbook steps** automatically to respond and prevent incidents  
   - Helps understand scope and root cause of threats

- SOAR also enables **proactive threat hunting** across data sources

---

### 3. **Key Concepts: Playbook & Runbook**
- **Playbook**  
  - Set of actions automating investigation & response  
  - Example given: email phishing playbook with conditional steps (high/low/moderate severity)

- **Runbook**  
  - Executes the playbook within the software  
  - Like a script that calls one or more playbooks  
  - Analogy: **Chef** automation software —  
    - Cookbook = Runbook  
    - Recipes = Playbooks  

- Terminology may vary by vendor, but the function is consistent.

---

### 4. **Exam Relevance (CISSP)**
- Know **purpose of SOAR**  
- Understand **purpose of playbook and runbook**  
- No need to memorize detailed playbook structures (example from D3 Security just for illustration)

---

```Welcome to this video on Behavior Analytics. On the CISSP exam, you may be asked questions about user and entity behavior analytics. So we're going to cover that here in this video. Now, behavior analytics is just the analysis of subject activity to detect potential threats. That's all we're really looking to do. We're looking to analyze how subjects are behaving on the system, and that will allow us to detect possible threats, potential threats. Specifically we're looking at their behavior, what they're doing on the system, how they're using devices, and also any security related events that are coming from that activity. So, behavior analytics is also known as User Behavior Analytics, or UBA. You can also refer to it as User and Entity Behavior Analytics, or UEBA, okay? Now, there's also network behavior analytics. There's a lot of different versions of this. What's most important is to understand that we're comparing the user or device behavior to past information, and that will help us detect anomalies. For example, when you're on a workstation, your job on a workstation is to perform work, right? You're going to log in and you're going to remote into a server, or you're going to open an application that's going to make an API call to a server or an application on the backend or a cloud-based service, or something, right? This is all normal behavior. This is all normal activity. So, at this point, what if, all of a sudden, from a workstation, you start getting a vulnerability scan? Well, that's kind of weird because we don't run scans from the workstations, we run 'em from our vulnerability server. So in this case, we're starting to pay attention to the user's activity on workstations or servers or whatever endpoint device is going to be connected up to the network. It could be mobile devices, could be IoTs, whatever it is, right? And then in this case, we're going to build some kind of a profile to start monitoring this. It's the same thing as like behavior-based intrusion detection, also behavior-based anti-malware detection, right? We're monitoring the activity, and that activity's going to tell us a story, and that story's going to be used to determine is this a threat or not? And this will help you uncover privileged account abuse, privileged escalation abuse, things like that. It will also help you detect data exfiltration attempts or otherwise missed data exfiltration events that maybe the data loss prevention software wasn't configured to find, right? Because now we're looking at all these different points of data from all these endpoints and everything else, and we're using those to conduct that behavior analysis. So in this case, we're sending all these logs everywhere, and we're sending them to say, a SIEM, a security information and event manager, something like Elastic Stack or AlienVault or RSA, there's a bunch of them out there. But we're going to send them there, and then this SIEM system can do the behavior analytics for us, it can perform this, right? So this is your best defense against unknown attacks, especially when it comes to attacks that kind of go unseen, like stealth attacks, where maybe you don't notice them with your normal mechanisms. If you're really doing good, solid behavior analytics, this will help you detect those attacks that might get missed by an IDS, IPS, DLP, some kind of other endpoint security. Another really good tool that performs behavior analytics is Splunk. Now, Splunk will do identity logs, it'll do device logs, DNS logs, application logs, database logs, network logs, you know, break room logs. It doesn't really matter. They will capture all of the data that you send to it. And Splunk can also help detect unknown threats and anomalous behavior using machine learning. Now, anomalous just basically means an anomaly or abnormal behavior, right? Things out of the norm. And it can help with advanced threat detection where you're looking at abnormal or unknown threats. It can help with higher productivity, where you're putting together a lot of different anomalies into a single threat profile, and then you're looking at it from that perspective, and that can accelerate your threat hunting through deep investigation capabilities and a lot of other things. So Splunk is very good at this, AlienVault's very good at this, RSA does a great job. There's a lot of great tools out there that do this. But the reality here is instead of just looking at your logs and relying on your endpoint security, you're now digging deeper into the logs and looking at multiple points of information, not just logins and logoffs, and success and unsuccess in terms of trying to make connections. Now you're looking at multiple points of behavior from different users and different subjects and machines and those kinds of things, and that's going to help you with that advanced-level threat detection, and that's the benefit of behavior analytics. So, the bottom line here for this video and for the exam is just to understand the purpose and the benefits of behavior analytics. You don't need to know all the ins and outs, and certainly remember that CISSP is vendor neutral, so you don't need to know Splunk or Elastic or RSA, don't need to know the vendors, just need to understand the concepts and the benefits behind behavior analytics.```

Here’s a structural summary of the video transcript on **Behavior Analytics** for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Definition & Purpose
- **Behavior analytics** = analysis of subject activity to detect potential threats.
- Focuses on:
  - How subjects behave on systems.
  - Device usage.
  - Security-related events from that activity.

## 2. Terminology
- Also called:
  - **UBA** (User Behavior Analytics)
  - **UEBA** (User and Entity Behavior Analytics)
- Related but distinct: **Network behavior analytics**.

## 3. Core Mechanism
- Compare current user/device behavior to **past behavior**.
- Detect **anomalies** (e.g., a workstation running a vulnerability scan).

## 4. What It Helps Detect
- Privileged account abuse
- Privilege escalation abuse
- Data exfiltration (including misses by DLP)

## 5. How It Works in Practice
- Logs from endpoints, servers, IoT, mobile devices → sent to a **SIEM**.
- SIEM performs behavior analytics.
- Example SIEM tools mentioned (vendor context, not required for exam):
  - Elastic Stack, AlienVault, RSA, **Splunk** (uses machine learning for unknown threats).

## 6. Key Benefits
- Best defense against **unknown/stealth attacks**.
- Catches what IDS/IPS/DLP/endpoint security might miss.
- Enables advanced threat detection by correlating multiple anomalies into a threat profile.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Configuration Management (CM)** :

### 1. Core Definition & Purpose
- **Configuration Management (CM):** Activities ensuring system components maintain a *known* configuration state.
- **Primary Goal:** Prevent unauthorized changes to systems.
- **Configuration:** Specifications/settings of an asset (server, firewall, etc.), including architecture design (interfaces, connections).

### 2. Key Terminology
- **Configuration Item (CI):** The asset that requires configuration control.
- **Change Control:** A related but separate topic (covered in next video).
- **CM Plan:** Defines *how* the organization manages/configures changes to assets.
- **CM Policy vs. Plan:** Policy = intention; Plan = execution (purpose, scope, roles, processes).

### 3. NIST SP 800-128 Framework (4 Phases)

| Phase | Key Activities |
|-------|----------------|
| **1. Planning** | Identify CIs (scope) → Create CM policy/processes → Establish a **Change Control Board (CCB)** (review/approve changes). CCB ensures separation of duties. |
| **2. Identifying & Implementing** | Define **secure baseline configuration** (specifications/version). Use versions for consistent deployment. **Provisioning** = create/manage/destroy CIs (can be automated via DevOps tools like Chef, Puppet, Ansible). |
| **3. Controlling** | Maintain secure baseline → Conduct security impact assessments for changes → Update CM plan & baseline documentation. |
| **4. Monitoring** | Analyze compliance with approved baselines (using integrity tools: AIDE, Tripwire, discovery/vulnerability scans). Identify unauthorized changes & improve CM processes. |

### 4. Important Concepts
- **Not everything is a CI** – only assets requiring control.
- **CCB composition:** Designated members + guest SMEs (e.g., network engineer for network changes).
- **Baseline versions** enable recovery, consistent deployment, and risk awareness.
- **Automation** (DevOps/DevSecOps) allows approved baselines to be provisioned without repeated security analysis.

### 5. Exam Takeaway
Understand the **purpose of CM**, key terms (CI, baseline, provision), and the **4-phase CM process** (Plan → Identify/Implement → Control → Monitor).

---

## 1. Definition & Purpose
- **Patch**: Fix for a known functionality problem in software/firmware (bug fixes, new features, security updates).
- **Patch Management**: Consistent process to identify and install patches while avoiding operational impact.
- **Link to Vulnerability Management**: Patches often fix vulnerabilities.

---

## 2. Key Policy & Process Elements
- **Patch management policy** must outline:
  - Identification, acquisition, installation, responsibilities.
  - Avoiding production/operations impact.
- **Key challenges**: timeliness, priority setting, testing before deployment.

---

## 3. When Patching Is Not Possible
- Options if a system/application cannot be patched:
  - Reconfigure (disable vulnerable service).
  - Remove the application.
  - Apply **compensating controls** (e.g., whitelisting, TLS encryption).
- Requires quick risk analysis.

---

## 4. Patch Management Architectures

| Approach | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Agent-based (centralized)** | Agents on hosts communicate with internal patch server → most common & effective. |
| **Agentless** | Server scans systems to detect missing patches. |
| **Passive network monitoring** | Monitors local network traffic to identify patching needs (limited to protocol-level visibility). |
| **Decentralized** | Hosts manage own patches → not recommended (loss of configuration control & baseline). |

- **NIST SP 800-40r3** comparison highlights: agent-based needs admin privileges, supports remote hosts, most effective overall.

---

## 5. General Steps of Patch Management
1. **Evaluate** – Identify relevant patches from trusted sources (e.g., NIST, vendors).
2. **Test** – Assess for negative impacts in sandbox/dev environment.
3. **Approve** – Submit to change control board (part of change/config management).
4. **Deploy** – Install in production as soon as possible to reduce risk exposure.
5. **Verify** – Confirm effectiveness and no operational issues (security tests, audits).

---

## 6. Bottom Line for Exam
- Understand **purpose & challenges** of patch management.
- Know **architectures** (agent-based vs. agentless vs. passive monitoring).
- Memorize the **5 general steps** (Evaluate → Test → Approve → Deploy → Verify).

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Change Control**:

## 1. Terminology & Relationship to Configuration Management
- **Change Management** and **Change Control** are interchangeable terms (NIST uses "change control").
- **Configuration Management (CM)** is the overarching 4-phase process:
  1. Planning
  2. Identifying & implementing configurations
  3. **Controlling configuration changes** ← Change control lives here
  4. Monitoring
- Change control applies to any **Configuration Item (CI)** : computer, app, server, firewall, mobile device, switch, router, etc.

## 2. The Change Control Process (7 Steps)

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1. **Request** | Formally request & record proposed change (ticket/form required for documentation) |
| 2. **Review** | Change Control Board (CCB) reviews impact |
| 3. **Build & Test** | Done in a development environment; identify security/functional impacts |
| 4. **Approve/Reject** | CCB decides based on test results (approve, approve with modifications, or reject) |
| 5. **Implement** | Deploy approved change without impacting **Ops** (government/federal) or **Prod** (commercial) – same meaning |
| 6. **Verify** | Confirm correct implementation; document new CI configuration |
| 7. **Close Out** | Update baseline, CM plan, all documentation → roll to new baseline version |

## 3. Flow of Roles
- **Requester** → documents change request
- **CCB** → reviews, then approves/rejects after testing
- **Engineers / Admins / Security Engineers** → build, test, implement
- **CCB** → final verification & close-out

## 4. Security Impact Analysis (Key Activities within Change Control)
- **Release control** – part of implementation step
- **Security impact analysis** includes:
  - Identify potential security risks/impacts
  - Discover vulnerabilities in software/hardware/assets affected by the change
  - Assess risks from threats/vulnerabilities
  - Assess impact on existing security/privacy controls and overall security posture
  - Perform **regression testing** (ensure change doesn't break other system parts)
- **Plan safeguards & countermeasures** – reduce risk to acceptable level (proactive + reactive)
- **Follow change control process** to update the security baseline (build security in early, not after deployment)

## 5. Bottom Line (Exam Focus)
- Know the **purpose** of change management/control
- Understand the **process** (request → review → build/test → approve → implement → verify → close out)
- Understand the **security impact analysis process**

### 1. Core Definition & Purpose
- **Software CM** ensures software maintains a *known configuration*.
- Critical for large and enterprise-level environments.
- Focuses on the software side (vs. general CM covered elsewhere).

### 2. Key Components of Software CM

| Component | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Configuration Items (CIs)** | System/software assets requiring control (e.g., OS, hypervisor). Identified in the CM plan. |
| **Baselines** | Pre-configured CIs used as a consistent starting point. Tested, verified, then versioned (e.g., 1.1.2 → 1.1.3). |
| **Versions** | Uniquely identify functionality or baseline configuration. |
| **Change Sets** | Collective changes made to a baseline as part of a change request. |
| **Branches** | Configurations built alongside the baseline (a "build in progress"). Checking out a baseline creates a branch; checking it back in (after CCB approval) creates a new official baseline. |

### 3. The Change Management Process (3 Sub-processes)

| Sub-process | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Request Control** | Procedures for *requesting* a change. |
| **Change Control** | Procedures for *identifying* the appropriate change (what's in the change set, which branch). |
| **Release Control** | Procedures for *deploying* the change to production/operations (pushing/rolling out). |

### 4. Step-by-Step Change Workflow
1. **Request** – Submit change to Change Control Board (CCB).
2. **Review** – Assess relevance, risk, impact.
3. **Build & Test** – Create proof of concept (still under change control).
4. **Approve/Reject** – CCB decides based on test results.
5. **Implement** – Push/roll out to production/ops (release control).
6. **Verify** – Check for negative impacts.
7. **Close Out** – Roll new baseline/version.

### 5. Key Benefits & Takeaways
- **Traceability & Accountability** – Multiple personnel involved at each step (requesters, testers, CCB, admins).
- **Governance** – If something fails, documentation allows rollback to previous baseline.
- **Bottom Line** – Understand the purpose of software CM and clearly understand the change management process.

### 1. Definition of Media  
- Any medium capable of storing data (HDD, SSD, tape, CD, DVD, mobile device, thumb drive, etc.).

### 2. Core Security Goal  
- Maintain **confidentiality, integrity, availability (CIA)** of data on media at all times.

### 3. Media Lifecycle & Availability  
- Media has a **finite lifespan** (mean time to failure).  
- Aging media can slow data retrieval → impacts **availability**.  
- Need **good inventory & asset tracking** to replace media before failure.

### 4. Relationship to Data Lifecycle  
- Media management focuses on the **storage phase** of the data lifecycle.  
- Data is created → labeled → stored on media → accessed → transferred to other media.

### 5. Marking & Labeling Assets (Critical)  
- **Physical marking** (e.g., “Secret” sticker on a hard drive) → identifies sensitivity/classification of data the media may contain.  
- **Digital labeling** (metadata, hard-coded) → ensures proper handling across systems.

### 6. Removable Media & Physical Controls  
- Use stickers, tags, markers.  
- **Encrypt** wherever possible.  
- Backup tapes → store in safes, lockable containers, vaults.  
- Media leaving facility → apply security controls for **transit/transport** protection.

### 7. Sanitization  
- When media is no longer needed → **properly sanitize** to prevent data remnant recovery.  
- Critical before reusing media at a lower classification level.

### 8. Proactive Replacement  
- Replace media before mean time to failure is realized.  
- Part of **continuous monitoring** and **asset security** to avoid availability loss or single points of failure.

### 9. Bottom Line  
- Understand the **purpose of media management**: protecting media throughout its lifecycle to uphold CIA.

Based on the transcript, here is a structural summary of the **Incident Management** process as presented, aligned with both the CISSP Common Body of Knowledge (CBK) and the NIST 800-61 framework.

### I. Core Definition
- **Incident:** An event (intentional or unintentional) that violates security policy.
- **Goal:** Manage, respond to, and recover from events that negatively impact the system.

### II. Key Frameworks (for reference)
- **Primary (Exam Focus):** NIST SP 800-61 (Rev 2) – *Computer Security Incident Handling Guide*.
- **Secondary:** ISO 27035, ISACA guides.

### III. The Incident Response Lifecycle (CISSP CBK Order)

#### 1. Detection
- **Sources:** System logs, IDS/IPS, endpoint security (firewalls), **personnel reports**.
- **Action:** Analyze events to verify if they constitute a security incident per policy.
- **Triage:** Determine severity and prioritize treatment (medical term adapted for security).

#### 2. Response
- **Trigger:** Based on severity level defined in the Incident Response Plan.
- **Team Activation:** CIRT (Computer Incident Response Team) or CSIRT.
- **Key Actions:**
    - Control damage/disruption.
    - Identify, collect, and handle evidence.
    - Thoroughly document everything.

#### 3. Mitigation
- **Purpose:** Quickly contain the incident to prevent further organizational impact.
- **Example:** Shutting down a port, isolating a network segment, blacklisting an IP.
- **Consideration:** Determine if Disaster Recovery (DR) or Business Continuity (BC) procedures are needed.

#### 4. Reporting
- **Timing:** After containment, not before (to avoid incomplete information).
- **Audiences:**
    - **Internal:** Senior management (status, impact, recovery timeline).
    - **External:** Required by regulations (e.g., GDPR mandates 72-hour breach notification).
- **Caution:** Exclude sensitive vulnerability/threat details from public reports.

#### 5. Recovering
- **Nature:** Temporary restoration to an operational state to prevent business impact.
- **Examples:** Re-enabling a network connection, restoring a system account, bringing a component back online.
- **Contingency:** If recovery exceeds MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime), activate BCP/DRP.

#### 6. Remediation
- **Nature:** Permanent restoration to full operational status.
- **Scope:** Address system damage, legal matters, financial impacts (e.g., investigation fees).

#### 7. Lessons Learned
- **Purpose:** Post-incident analysis to improve future response.
- **Key Questions:**
    - What happened and why?
    - What could have prevented it?
    - What can stakeholders do differently?
- **Output:** Update plans, controls, and monitor changes for effectiveness.

### IV. Foundational Preparations (Pre-Detection)
- **Policy:** Define objectives, scope, what constitutes an incident, priorities, KPIs/KRIs, and reporting requirements.
- **Resources:** Deploy tools (DLP, firewalls, storage), establish recovery sites.
- **Team:** Form a cohesive CIRT with appropriate skills (sysadmins, network, security, management).
- **Procedures:** Create step-by-step responses for possible scenarios; get buy-in from system owners and senior management.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on security investigations for the CSSP exam:

### 1. Core Purpose of an Investigation
- **Goal:** Collect and analyze facts about an event to reach a conclusion (determine if something did or did not happen).
- **Your Role:** Primarily a *support role* (collecting evidence, maintaining chain of custody, possibly testifying in court), unless you are a forensic investigator or the sole security professional.

### 2. Key Concepts & Terminology
- **Burden of Proof:** The obligation to prove the event took place (or didn't).
    - *Criminal proceeding:* Proof **beyond a reasonable doubt** (to a jury of peers).
    - *Civil proceeding:* **Preponderance of evidence** (majority/more likely than not).
- **Parties involved:**
    - *Criminal:* Plaintiff (accuser) vs. Defendant.
    - *Civil:* Claimant vs. Respondent.
- **Chain of Custody:** Must protect evidence and maintain an accurate record of who handled it and how.

### 3. Investigative Techniques
- **Interviewing:** Talking to personnel (admins, engineers, etc.) to gather information.
- **Interrogation:** A specific, more focused interview to determine if a subject committed a violation (usually for law enforcement, but usable in internal investigations).
- **Surveillance:** Monitoring a subject (e.g., via real-time logs, CCTV) to gather more evidence.
- **Digital Forensics:** Identifying, collecting, analyzing, and preserving electronic data from servers, workstations, endpoints, etc.

### 4. Types of Investigations (for the exam)
- **Administrative:** Violation of *organizational policy*.
- **Regulatory (Compliance):** Violation of a *law or regulation*.
- **Criminal:** Violation of *laws* (country/state level).
- **Civil:** Private or non-criminal matters (e.g., breach of contract, SLA, user agreement).

### 5. Investigative Mindset: *Modus Operandi* (Mode of Operations)
Focus on finding the root cause by examining three factors:
1.  **Motive:** Why did they do it?
2.  **Opportunity:** When and where could they do it?
3.  **Means:** Did they have the capability, tools, and techniques?

### 6. Exam Bottom Line
- The **accuser** (plaintiff/claimant) always has the burden of proof.
- Understand the different types of investigations at a high level (not how to execute them in detail).

Here’s a **structural summary** of the video on *Evidence Collection and Handling* for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Purpose of Evidence
- **Definition**: Facts/data proving an incident occurred.
- **Goal**: Demonstrate a security incident occurred; prove/disprove root cause.
- **Admissibility**: Evidence must be directly relevant to the incident; judge decides admissibility based on laws/regulations.

---

## 2. Types of Evidence

| Type | Description | Examples |
|------|-------------|----------|
| **Real** | Tangible objects | Fingerprints on keyboard, video recording, screen scrape |
| **Documentary** | Written proof of facts/statements | Audit logs, entry/exit logs (must be authenticated) |
| **Testimonial** | Written/verbal witness statements | Witness describing what they saw |
| **Demonstrative** (corroborating) | Helps demonstrate testimony | Diagrams, models, supporting evidence |
| **Direct** | Witness directly observed the offense | Saw attacker typing commands |
| **Hearsay** | Secondhand knowledge (“someone told me”) | “John told me he saw the attacker” |
| **Opinion** | Expert statement | Forensic analyst explaining attack method |
| **Circumstantial** | Facts combined to infer offense | Multiple indirect clues pointing to guilt |
| **Corroborative** | Supports/validates a claim | Video + logs matching hearsay statement |

---

## 3. Key Legal Rules

- **Best Evidence Rule**: Use **original** documentation whenever possible; copies are **secondary evidence** (less admissible, harder to authenticate).
- **Parol Evidence Rule**: Verbal agreements about evidence must be put **in writing** to become documentary evidence.

---

## 4. Chain of Custody (Critical)
- **Definition**: Proper handling, marking, tracking of each piece of evidence.
- **Why vital**: Breaks in chain introduce doubt → evidence may be thrown out.
- **Document** for every transfer:
  - What was transferred (hard drive, logs, etc.)
  - Who transferred to whom
  - When (date/time to seconds)
  - How (physical, digital, envelope, etc.)
  - Signatures of **both parties** for custody change

---

## 5. Collection Best Practices
- Get a **second opinion** / second person present during witness interviews.
- Avoid **investigator bias** (don’t try to prove a preconceived narrative).
- **Document everything**: IP addresses, nodes, rooms, buildings—nothing is overkill.

---

## 6. Example Scenario (Insider Threat)
- **Real**: Thumb drive, video footage  
- **Documentary**: Audit logs  
- **Testimonial/Direct**: Sysadmin witnessed act  
- **Hearsay**: Coworker heard argument but didn’t see  
- **Opinion**: External web admin forensic analysis  
- **Circumstantial**: Employee saw insider in data center  
- **Corroborative**: Access logs + video of entry

---

## 7. Bottom Line for CISSP
- Know the **different types of evidence**.
- Understand the **purpose and mechanics of chain of custody**.
- Apply **best evidence rule** and **parol evidence rule** appropriately.

- **BC** = keeping business operations running.

Here’s a **structured summary** of the video transcript on *Disaster Recovery Strategies*:

---

## 1. Core Concepts
- **Disaster**: Event causing major damage/destruction (facility, resources, property, or life).
- **Business Continuity**: Focuses on **critical business functions**.
- **Disaster Recovery**: Focuses on **assets supporting those functions**.

---

## 2. Key Recovery Strategies

| Strategy | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **System Resilience** | System’s ability to recover from disruption; minimizes single points of failure. |
| **Fault Tolerance** | System continues operating *during* a failure (built into system). |
| **High Availability** | Uses redundant systems (servers, apps) for quick recovery over long periods. |

> Resilience is the umbrella term; fault tolerance & HA are sub-types.

---

## 3. Data Protection: RAID Levels

| RAID Level | Name | Fault Tolerance | Description |
|------------|------|----------------|-------------|
| RAID‑0 | Striping | ❌ No | Data split across disks; performance only. |
| RAID‑1 | Mirroring | ✅ Yes | Identical copies on 2 disks; resource‑intensive. |
| RAID‑5 | Striping with parity | ✅ Yes | 3+ disks, one for parity; slower if a disk fails. |
| RAID‑10 | Stripe of mirrors | ✅ Yes | 4+ disks; combines striping & mirroring. |

---

## 4. Server & Network Resilience

- **Failover Cluster**: Multiple servers/nodes share workload; if one fails, others take over.
- **Load Balancing**: Distributes traffic/processes across servers (via load balancer or cluster).

---

## 5. Power Protection

| Solution | Duration | Notes |
|----------|----------|-------|
| **UPS** (uninterruptible power supply) | Short period | Battery or flywheel; needs space inside data center. |
| **Generator** | Long period | Motor‑driven; needs fuel & maintenance. |

**Additional**: Voltage regulators, line conditioners, surge protectors.

---

## 6. Network Communications: QoS
**Quality of Service (QoS)** prioritizes critical traffic on limited‑capacity networks.  
Handles: throughput, bandwidth, latency, jitter, errors.  
Requires: traffic identification → classification → device configuration.

---

## 7. Failure States (Critical for Firewalls & Network Devices)

| State | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **Fail open** | Defaults to allowing all access during failure (insecure). |
| **Fail safe / fail secure** | Defaults to allowing nothing; system stays secure. |

> Always design devices to **fail in a secure state** (closed).

---

## 8. Integrated Example (from diagram description)
- Redundant switches, servers, load balancers → failover / HA.
- RAID for storage redundancy.
- UPS or generator for power outages.
- QoS for traffic prioritization under stress.

---

## 9. Bottom Line (Exam Takeaways)
- Know recovery methods (resilience, fault tolerance, HA).
- Know protection methods (RAID, failover clusters, power protection).
- Understand QoS and failure states (fail safe vs. fail open).

Here’s a structural summary of the video transcript on **disaster recovery sites** for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Purpose of a Recovery Site (Alternate Processing Site)
- Used temporarily after a disaster or major disruption at the primary site.
- Focuses on **IT assets** (networks, servers, databases, etc.) supporting business functions.
- Not for permanent relocation; typical duration = days (depends on disaster severity and stakeholder-defined tolerances).

---

## 2. Selection Criteria
- Based on **Business Impact Analysis (BIA)** results, especially **Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD)**.
- Also considers **Recovery Time Objective (RTO)** and budget.

---

## 3. Types of Recovery Sites

| Site Type | Infrastructure / Equipment | Data | Cost | Activation Time |
|-----------|---------------------------|------|------|----------------|
| **Cold Site** | Empty room/warehouse; no computing equipment | None | Lowest | Days to weeks |
| **Warm Site** | Pre-configured computing equipment, basic infrastructure (HVAC, electricity, patch/baseline servers) | No operational data (only system data) | Moderate | ~12 hours |
| **Hot Site** | Full suite: computers, networks, near-real-time data, full infrastructure | Near real-time (copied daily/hourly) | Very high | Minutes to a few hours |

---

## 4. Other Recovery Options

- **Mobile Site**  
  - Self-contained, transportable (shipping container, tractor-trailer).  
  - Typically configured as **cold or warm** site.  
  - Contains critical assets; can be moved geographically.

- **Cloud-Managed Recovery Site**  
  - Hosted on AWS, Azure, GCP, etc.  
  - Usually **warm or hot**.  
  - Key: **SLA** defines roles, availability, performance, data rates, costs (metered by VM uptime).

- **Shared Site**  
  - Shared with one or more external organizations.  
  - Governed by **Mutual Assistance Agreement (MAA)** or reciprocal agreement.  
  - Rare due to data sensitivity and legal issues.

---

## 5. Critical Requirement
- **Geographic isolation** from the primary site (e.g., different city/region) to avoid the same disaster impacting both sites.

---

## 6. Exam Takeaway
- Know **purpose** of recovery sites.  
- Understand **what is present** at cold, warm, hot, mobile, cloud, and shared sites.  
- Activation time and cost are inversely related to readiness.

---

## 1. Core Purpose of Backup
- Duplicate data to retrieve it later after data loss or system failure.
- Critical for disaster recovery (DR).

## 2. Key Concepts
- **Mirroring**: Identical copy on ≥2 storage media (e.g., RAID).
- **Archive bit (backup bit)**:  
  - `0` = backed up (no change since last backup).  
  - `1` = needs backup (file changed).

## 3. Backup Types

| Type | What it does | Archive bit after backup |
|------|--------------|--------------------------|
| **Full** | Complete copy of all data | Sets all to `0` |
| **Differential** | Changes since **last full backup** | Does not reset (leaves `1`) |
| **Incremental** | Changes since **any last backup** (full/diff/inc) | Resets to `0` |

- **Full**: large, infrequent (e.g., Sundays).
- **Differential**: medium, captures everything since last full.
- **Incremental**: small, frequent (e.g., daily except full/diff days).

## 4. 3-2-1 Backup Rule
- **3** copies of data.
- **2** different devices/media on-premise.
- **1** copy off-premise.

## 5. Off-Premise Backup (Electronic Vaulting)
- **Remote journaling**: logs + metadata off-site (for audit/analysis).
- **Remote mirroring**: real-time streaming of changes off-site.
- Recovery needs both **journal** + backup data.

## 6. Storage Media
- Disks, tapes, external drives — no mandated method (org chooses).

## 7. Snapshots
- Virtual copies of files, dirs, volumes, VMs (e.g., via hypervisor).

## 8. Escrow Arrangements
- **Key/certificate escrow**: third-party agent stores crypto keys; recovery agent accesses.
- **Software escrow**: stores source code, licenses, docs — protects if vendor fails.

## 9. Rotation Schedules (historical exam topics)
- FIFO, Grandfather-Father-Son, Tower of Hanoi.
- Key point: ensure chosen schedule meets **compliance retention requirements** (1, 3, 5, 10 years, etc.).

## 10. Exam Takeaway
Know:
- Backup types (full, diff, inc) + archive bit behavior.
- Electronic vaulting methods.
- Escrow arrangements (key/cert, software).

Based on the video transcript, here is a structured summary of the **disaster recovery processes**:

### 1. Core Focus & Definition
- **Goal:** Ensure critical business assets and processes (IT infrastructure: servers, workstations, databases, websites) remain operational after a disruption.
- **Scope:** Applies to on-premise, off-premise (remote/cloud), local, or remote assets.
- **Reference Standard:** NIST SP 800-34 (Contingency Planning Guide).

### 2. Priority Hierarchy
1.  **Human Life (Top Priority):** Safety and security of personnel overrides all technology concerns.
2.  **Communication:** Essential for assessing safety and coordinating response.
3.  **Technology Recovery:** Only after human safety is addressed.

### 3. Key Processes within the DRP

| Process | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Documentation** | Assign a scribe/spokesperson as single point of contact for clear, consistent communication with management, emergency services, and media. |
| **Training & Awareness** | Ensure team members know roles, responsibilities, first aid, fire suppression, crisis management, evidence collection, and collaboration with law enforcement/emergency services. |
| **Response** | Define procedures based on disaster type (natural or manmade). Activate the **Business Continuity Plan (BCP)** if Recovery Time Objective (RTO) or Recovery Point Objective (RPO) cannot be met. |
| **Personnel** | Define roles, responsibilities, response times, and **primary/alternate (backup)** personnel for each role to account for absence due to the disaster. |
| **Communications** | Use a single recognizable voice to relay activation status, situation updates, and instructions internally and externally (media, law enforcement). Maintain a contact information table. |
| **Assessment** | Investigate disruption extent, impact on tolerance levels (RTO/RPO), sales, reputation, contracts, legal/regulatory compliance, and risk to human life. Triage the situation. |
| **Restoration** | Move operations back to the **original primary location** (vs. recovery = bringing systems back to normal at any site). Restore **least critical functions first** to avoid impacting critical operations if a failure recurs. |
| **Lessons Learned** | Evaluate personnel performance, team speed, tolerance impacts, communication effectiveness. Identify what went right/wrong and corrective actions for future prevention, detection, and response. |

### 4. Key Exam Takeaways
- **BCP vs. DRP:** BCP identifies critical business functions and drives the overall plan; DRP is a subset focused on **recovering the technology infrastructure** that supports those functions.
- **Top Priority:** Always choose human life first in any exam question.
- **Recovery vs. Restoration:**
    - *Recovery* = bringing systems back to normal condition (possibly at alternate site).
    - *Restoration* = returning systems to original state at primary location.

---

## 1. Context & Key Definitions
- **Disaster Recovery (DR)** → Ensures critical *technological* assets/processes stay operational after a disruption.
- **Business Continuity (BC)** → Focuses on *critical business functions*.
- DR supports BC → The difference between BCP and DRP.

---

## 2. Key Reference Document for CISSP
- **NIST SP 800-84** – Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities.
- Two main exercise types:
  - **Tabletop exercise** – Discuss roles, responsibilities, responses.

---

## 3. Disaster Recovery Tests (in order of increasing complexity/impact)

| Test | Description | Production Impact? |
|------|-------------|--------------------|
| **Read-through test** (checklist test) | Review DRP, redline updates, agree on roles/responsibilities. | ❌ No |
| **Walkthrough test** (tabletop) | Structured meeting, rehearse procedures, coordinate scenarios (fire, flood, cyber, etc.). | ❌ No |
| **Simulation test** (preparedness test) | Role-play realistic conditions on-prem (evacuation drills, system activation). No relocation. | ❌ No |
| **Parallel test** | Activate recovery site using DRP; primary site runs normal ops. Tests external services/SLAs. | ❌ No |
| **Full interruption test** | Simulate disaster, migrate primary operations to recovery site. Requires senior management approval. Conducted off-peak hours. | ✅ **Yes** |

---

## 4. Post-Testing Actions
- Redline and update BCP/DRP.
- Put through **Configuration Management (CM)** process.
- Continuous monitoring: changes in processes, personnel, regulations → trigger plan review.
- Ensure DRP supports BCP (target correct servers, apps, etc.).

## 5. Exam Key Takeaway
- Only the **full interruption test** impacts production/operations.  
- All other tests are designed to avoid disruption.
